passages.t: Lot takes two strangers into his house
passages.happening:
“Now the two angels arrived at Sodom in the evening, and Lot was sitting in the gateway of the city” (verse 1). When Lot sees them, he gets up and bows with his face to the ground.

He invites them in: “please turn aside into the house of your servant; wash your feet and spend the night” (verse 2). They can leave early in the morning. They answer, “we will spend the night in the square” (verse 2).

“But Lot insisted so strongly that they followed him into his house” (verse 3). He makes them a meal and bakes bread without yeast, and they eat.
passages.hearers:
These are two of the three visitors who came to Abraham in the last chapter. Two of them went on toward Sodom while Abraham stayed to plead with the LORD (18:22). Chapter 18 called them men. Here they are called angels. The Hebrew word means ‘messengers’: they come on God's errand.

The gate of an ancient town was more than a door in the wall. Elders sat there, people traded there, and cases were judged there (Ruth 4:1-2). So Lot sitting in the gate suggests he has become a man of some standing in Sodom. Watch how far he has come. In chapter 13 he pitched his tent ‘toward Sodom’ (13:12). In chapter 14 he was living in it (14:12). Now he sits in its gate.

The first hearers would set this scene beside the one before it. Abraham sat at his tent door at noon. Lot sits at the city gate in the evening. Both men get up, bow and offer welcome. Abraham ran and served a feast. Lot serves a quick meal. Bread without yeast is bread made in a hurry, with no time to wait for the dough to rise.

The square was the open space inside the gate. Why does Lot press the strangers so hard not to sleep there? He knows his city. The reader is about to find out.
passages.later:
Hebrews remembers this kind of welcome: “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it” (Hebrews 13:2). Hospitality means welcoming a stranger and giving them food, shelter and safety.

The book of Judges tells a story much like this one, set in Gibeah, a town in Israel. A traveler sits in the town square at evening, “but no one would take them into his home for the night” (Judges 19:15). An old man takes him in. What follows is like Sodom. The Bible is saying that Israel itself could become Sodom.
passages.asks: Lot knew his city was dangerous for strangers, so he would not leave them in the square. Ask whether you know of a place where people are not safe: a street, a school, a part of town. Then ask what it would mean to open your door, as Lot did here.

passages.t: The men of the city at the door
passages.happening:
Before the guests go to bed, “all the men of the city of Sodom, both young and old, surrounded the house” (verse 4). They shout to Lot, “Where are the men who came to you tonight? Send them out to us so we can have relations with them!” (verse 5). They mean to rape the two guests.

Lot goes out and shuts the door behind him. “Please, my brothers,” he pleaded, “don’t do such a wicked thing!” (verse 7). Then he offers his two daughters to the crowd instead (verse 8). He says the men “have come under the protection of my roof” (verse 8).

The crowd turns on Lot: “This one came here as a foreigner, and he is already acting like a judge!” (verse 9). They push toward the door to break it down. The two guests pull Lot inside and shut the door. They strike the men outside with blindness, so that they wear themselves out trying to find the door (verses 10-11).
passages.hearers:
‘Have relations with’ translates the Hebrew word ‘know’. In Genesis it often means sexual intercourse (4:1). Verse 8 uses the same word of Lot's daughters, who have ‘never slept with a man’. So the crowd's demand is plain. They want to rape the strangers, by force, all of them together.

Notice who is there: ‘all the men of the city’, ‘young and old’. The whole town has come. That answers Abraham's prayer in the last chapter. He asked God to spare the city for ten righteous people (18:32). There were not ten.

In that world a host was bound to protect anyone under his roof. A guest was safe in your house the way a child is safe in your arms. Lot knows this. That is why he goes out to face the crowd alone and calls them ‘my brothers’, as if pleading with neighbors.

But the crowd reminds him what he is: a foreigner. Lot has lived in Sodom for years and sat in its gate. To them he is still an outsider who has no right to judge them.

Watch the door. Lot shuts it behind him. The crowd tries to break it. The angels pull Lot back and shut it. The blinded men cannot find it. The door is the line between the guests and the violence outside, and God keeps it shut.
passages.later:
Later Scripture names Sodom's sin more than once. Ezekiel says to Jerusalem, “Now this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: She and her daughters were arrogant, overfed, and complacent; they did not help the poor and needy” (Ezekiel 16:49). He adds, “Thus they were haughty and committed abominations before Me” (Ezekiel 16:50).

Isaiah calls Jerusalem's leaders “you rulers of Sodom” (Isaiah 1:10) and tells them to “seek justice and correct the oppressor” (Isaiah 1:17). Jude says the cities “indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh” (Jude 7). Jesus names Sodom when he speaks of a town that will not welcome his messengers: “it will be more bearable for Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for that town” (Matthew 10:15). In Luke 17 he speaks of ‘the days of Lot’ (see the note on verses 23-29).

Judges 19 tells a story nearly the same as this one, in Israel's own town of Gibeah (Judges 19:22-24). Later Jewish tradition, in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 109), remembered Sodom above all as a city that shut out strangers and punished kindness to the poor.

So the Bible names Sodom for pride, for ease while the poor went hungry, for cruelty to strangers and for sexual violence, together.
passages.hard:
Two hard things stand in these verses.

First, how do Christians read the sexual side of Sodom's sin? All agree that the men of Sodom tried to gang-rape two strangers, and that this was monstrous. They differ on one further question. The traditional reading, held by most churches through history, sees the same-sex nature of the demand as part of what the text condemns, along with the violence. Its holders point to Jude 7 and to Leviticus 18:22. Another reading holds that the whole point is violent cruelty to strangers, the worst possible breach of hospitality, and that the story does not speak to other questions. Its holders point out that Ezekiel, Isaiah and Jesus name pride, injustice and the refusal of welcome, and that Jude's ‘strange flesh’ (in Greek, ‘other flesh’) has been read by some as the angels. These notes take no side on that question here. On both readings nothing in this chapter gives anyone a reason for contempt toward any person.

Second, Lot offers his daughters (verse 8). This is wrong, and the text does not praise it. Lot is trying to protect his guests, but he tries to do it by handing over his own children to be raped. Genesis reports the offer without one word of approval. The crowd refuses it, and it is the angels, not Lot, who save the house. Judges 19 tells a darker version, where a woman is handed over to the crowd and is found at dawn lying at the door (Judges 19:25-27). Peter later calls Lot “a righteous man” (2 Peter 2:7), but that does not make everything he did right. Lot is saved by God's mercy (verse 16), not by his goodness.

A word for anyone who was not protected by a parent, or was handed over to harm by someone who should have kept them safe. This story does not call that right. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If you are still in danger, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The city came to Lot's door, and Lot, trying to do one right thing, offered a terrible wrong. Ask whether you have ever tried to protect one person by sacrificing someone weaker. Then ask who in your life most needs you to keep the door shut for them.

passages.happening:
The two men ask Lot whether he has anyone else in the city: sons-in-law, sons or daughters. “For the outcry to the LORD against its people is so great that He has sent us to destroy it” (verse 13).

Lot goes to the men pledged to marry his daughters. “Get up,” he said. “Get out of this place, for the LORD is about to destroy the city!” “But his sons-in-law thought he was joking” (verse 14).

At dawn the angels hurry Lot to take his wife and his two daughters and go (verse 15). “But when Lot hesitated, the men grabbed his hand and the hands of his wife and his two daughters” (verse 16). They lead them out of the city “because of the LORD’s compassion for them” (verse 16).

One of them says, “Run for your lives! Do not look back, and do not stop anywhere on the plain! Flee to the mountains, or you will be swept away!” (verse 17). Lot begs to go to a small town nearby instead (verses 18-20). The angel agrees, and tells him to hurry. The town is called Zoar (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
‘Pledged in marriage’ means the young men were promised to Lot's daughters by a binding agreement, but the weddings had not yet happened. The Hebrew can also be read as men who had already married daughters of Lot. If so, Lot had married daughters who stayed and died in the city.

‘Joking’ comes from the Hebrew word for laughing. It is the same root as Isaac's name, and as Abraham's and Sarah's laughter in the chapters before (17:17; 18:12). In Abraham's tent laughter met a promise of life. In Sodom it meets a warning of death.

Lot hesitates. The Hebrew word suggests dragging his feet. Even with fire coming, he cannot let go. So the angels take him by the hand and set him down outside the city like a child. ‘Compassion’ here means pity, the feeling that moves someone to spare another. Lot is not rescued because he was quick or brave. He is rescued because God pitied him.

Then Lot argues about where to go. He was told to flee to the mountains, and he asks for a small town on the plain. Even this request is granted. The name Zoar sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘small’, which Lot keeps saying: ‘is it not a small place?’ The angel even says he cannot act until Lot is safe. The judgment waits for one hesitating man.
passages.later:
The prophets use the picture of someone pulled out of a fire. God says to his people, “you were like a firebrand snatched from a blaze” (Amos 4:11). Zechariah asks, “Is not this man a firebrand snatched from the fire?” (Zechariah 3:2).

Peter draws a lesson from Lot's rescue: “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials” (2 Peter 2:9). And Jesus warns that on the day of the Son of Man, “let no one in the field return for anything he has left behind” (Luke 17:31).
passages.asks: Lot was dragged out of danger while he was still dragging his feet. Ask what you are slow to leave, even when you know it is harming you. Then notice that God did not wait for Lot to be brave. He took him by the hand.

passages.happening:
By the time the sun rises, Lot has reached Zoar (verse 23). “Then the LORD rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah” (verse 24). He destroys the cities, the whole plain, the people and everything that grew there (verse 25).

“But Lot’s wife looked back, and she became a pillar of salt” (verse 26).

Early the next morning Abraham goes back to the place where he had stood before the LORD. He looks down toward Sodom and Gomorrah and sees “the smoke rising from the land like smoke from a furnace” (verse 28).

The chapter sums it up: “He remembered Abraham, and He brought Lot out of the catastrophe that destroyed the cities where he had lived” (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Genesis places Sodom and Gomorrah in the plain of the Jordan, near the Dead Sea (13:10-12). It is a land of salt, tar and sulfur, and Genesis 14:10 mentions tar pits there. Where Sodom stood is not known. Some place it south of the Dead Sea; others north of it. Some have suggested a natural cause for the disaster, such as an earthquake setting the region's tar and gases on fire. The text tells it simply as the LORD's act.

On Mount Sodom, at the south-west of the Dead Sea, a pillar of salt rock is nicknamed ‘Lot's wife’. That is a later local name, not evidence.

‘Destroyed’ in these verses translates a Hebrew word meaning to overturn or overthrow. It became the Bible's standard word for Sodom's end, and the prophets use it again and again for total judgment.

Lot's wife ‘looked back’. The Hebrew says she looked ‘from behind him’, trailing behind her husband, and it uses the same word as the angel's command not to look back (verse 17). She did what she had been told not to do. Her heart seems to have stayed in the city.

‘He remembered Abraham’ uses the same words as ‘God remembered Noah’ in the flood (8:1). When God remembers in the Bible, he does not recall a forgotten fact. He acts on a promise. Lot is saved because Abraham prayed.
passages.later:
Jesus speaks of these days: “It was the same in the days of Lot: People were eating and drinking, buying and selling, planting and building. But on the day Lot left Sodom, fire and sulfur rained down from heaven and destroyed them all” (Luke 17:28-29). Then he says, “Remember Lot’s wife!” (Luke 17:32). His point follows: “Whoever tries to save his life will lose it” (Luke 17:33).

Moses warns that a land which turns from God could become “just like the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah” (Deuteronomy 29:23). Isaiah says, “Unless the LORD of Hosts had left us a few survivors, we would have become like Sodom” (Isaiah 1:9). Peter says God made the cities “an example of what is coming on the ungodly” (2 Peter 2:6).
passages.hard:
How can a good God destroy whole cities? Readers ask this, and they should.

Genesis has already let Abraham ask it: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (18:25). God agreed to spare the city for ten righteous people, and there were not ten. The ‘outcry’ against Sodom (18:20; 19:13) was the cry of people being wronged. God went to see before he acted. He pulled out every person who would come, and the sons-in-law who laughed were warned too.

Readers still ask about the children in the city. The text does not answer every question, and these notes will not pretend it does. What the Bible holds is that God is a just judge who sees everything. Jesus says the day of judgment will be ‘more bearable’ for Sodom than for towns that saw his works and turned away (Matthew 11:23-24). Many readers take that to mean God judges each person by what they knew.

The site's Honest Answer, ‘Did God command genocide in the Old Testament?’, faces the wider question of judgment in the Old Testament at more length.
passages.asks: Lot's wife was safely out of the city, but she could not stop looking back. Jesus says, ‘Remember Lot's wife.’ Ask what you keep looking back to, even after God has brought you out. Then ask what it would mean to face forward.

passages.happening:
Lot is afraid to stay in Zoar. He goes up into the mountains with his two daughters and lives in a cave (verse 30).

The older daughter says to the younger, “Our father is old, and there is no man in the land to sleep with us” (verse 31). They make their father drunk with wine, and on two nights, first the older and then the younger sleeps with him. Each time “he was not aware when she lay down or when she got up” (verses 33 and 35).

“Thus both of Lot’s daughters became pregnant by their father” (verse 36). The older has a son named Moab, “the father of the Moabites of today” (verse 37). The younger has a son named Ben-ammi, “the father of the Ammonites of today” (verse 38).
passages.hearers:
The daughters have lost their home, their mother and the men they were to marry. They may have believed that the whole world had been destroyed, as in the flood, or only that no one would marry the daughters of a man who ran from Sodom. In that world a woman with no husband and no children had little protection, and no one to care for her in old age. Their fear is real. What they do with it is wrong.

The first hearers would hear an echo of Noah. After the flood, Noah drank wine, lay uncovered, and shame came on his family through his children (9:20-27). After Sodom, Lot is made drunk, and the same kind of shame follows.

The man who once sat in the city gate now lives in a cave. Lot chose the well-watered plain because it looked good (13:10). He ends with nothing.

The name Moab sounds like the Hebrew for ‘from father’. Ben-ammi means ‘son of my kin’. The words ‘of today’ show that the writer lived when the Moabites and Ammonites were well known. They were real kingdoms east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. A stone inscription set up by a king of Moab named Mesha, from about the middle of the 800s BC, tells of his wars with Israel. The Bible tells of the same king (2 Kings 3:4-5).
passages.later:
Israel's later law forbids sex with a close relative: “None of you are to approach any close relative to have sexual relations” (Leviticus 18:6).

Yet God does not forget Lot's descendants. Moses says the LORD gave land “to the descendants of Lot as their possession”, and Israel was not to take it (Deuteronomy 2:9, 19). Later the Moabites and Ammonites were kept out of Israel's assembly because “they did not meet you with food and water” on the way out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 23:3-4).

And then comes Ruth. She is a Moabite woman (Ruth 1:4) who chooses Naomi's people and Naomi's God. She becomes the great-grandmother of King David (Ruth 4:17). Matthew names her in the family line of Jesus: “Boaz the father of Obed by Ruth” (Matthew 1:5). King Solomon's son Rehoboam had an Ammonite mother, “Naamah the Ammonite” (1 Kings 14:21). The line that began in a cave is taken into the line of the Messiah.
passages.hard:
Is this story approved? No. Genesis tells it briefly and plainly, and gives it no praise. The daughters did something wrong to their father, and Lot's drunkenness made him helpless. The story is the sad end of a family that settled in Sodom.

This story is also not a slur on a people. Moab and Ammon were later Israel's neighbors and often its enemies, but the Bible itself gives them their land and brings Ruth the Moabite into the family of Jesus. Nothing here is said against Moabites, Ammonites, or anyone living east of the Jordan today.

A word for anyone who has suffered sexual abuse within a family. This story does not call it right, and neither does the rest of the Bible. What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. If it is happening now, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Lot's story ends in a cave, and yet from that cave came Ruth, and from Ruth came David, and from David came Jesus. Ask whether there is a part of your family's story you are ashamed of. Then ask whether you believe God can bring something good out of it without calling the wrong good.
